conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Anything you share today stays between you and the care team, and there’s no judgment—just support. We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to begin?

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly... not really. I mean, I can smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or something, but the laughter that used to just bubble up—it's barely there. My husband tried to joke the other night and I could feel myself forcing a chuckle, but it felt flat. It’s like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Definitely not as much as I used to. I’ve managed a couple of weak chuckles—like when my mom sent that silly meme—but it feels forced and fades fast. Most of the time I’m too worn-out or just down to find things genuinely funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little outings or even just my morning coffee, but now it’s like, “what’s the point?” A couple of times I thought, “Maybe I’ll feel better if I go for a walk,” but when the moment comes I’m too tired and it just feels flat. I still go through the motions, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens pretty often. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m not comforting him well enough or I missed some cue. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat there crying, telling myself I’m wasting the one thing he needs from me. I know, logically, accidents happen, but my head keeps saying it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly my chest gets tight imagining him choking or that I’ll fall asleep and drop him. Sometimes I check the crib three times while he’s asleep—hand on his chest to feel him breathe—then I tiptoe back five minutes later. There isn’t always a clear trigger; the thoughts just loop and it’s hard to shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden rush—heart racing, can’t catch my breath—like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s going on. Once I was just folding laundry and I had to sit down because I felt like the room was closing in. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky and on edge. It’s scary when it hits out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered, and I think, “How am I supposed to keep doing this every single day?” I manage to push through, but I’m constantly on the edge of tears and it’s exhausting pretending I’ve got it together.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll lie down once the baby’s finally out, but my head just keeps spinning—did I sterilize the bottles right, what if he rolls over tonight, am I doing any of this good enough. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I jolt awake at every little sound. Last night I was still wide-eyed at 3 a.m., ended up crying quietly so I wouldn’t wake my husband.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud hanging over everything. I can still smile if someone talks to me, but the happiness fades in seconds and I’m back to feeling empty or teary. Some mornings I wake up already sad, before anything’s even happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve broken down a couple of times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap and I just sat on the nursery floor bawling while he fussed. It’s not all-day crying, but when the stress piles up I can’t hold it in. Feels like the tears come out of nowhere and then I’m exhausted after.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…Yeah. A couple of fleeting thoughts popped in this week—like when I was at my most overwhelmed, I caught myself thinking “what if I just weren’t here.” They were just quick flashes, no plan or anything, but they scared me. I don’t want to leave my baby; I just want the pressure inside me to stop.

You've shared how the joy and spark that used to come easily now feel distant-laughter is forced, simple pleasures like a walk or morning coffee feel pointless, and most days carry a gray, heavy sadness. You described frequent tearfulness, constant worry about your baby's safety even when nothing is wrong, sudden panicky moments, and nights spent wide-eyed with racing thoughts. Everyday tasks feel overwhelming, and you often blame yourself when things go imperfectly. You also mentioned fleeting thoughts of not wanting to be here, though you quickly emphasized you don't want to leave your baby-you just want the crushing pressure to stop. These feelings are understandably frightening and exhausting, and they highlight how much you're carrying right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter and a clear reduction from pre-pregnancy enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—no spark despite trying to engage—matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent self-blame for normal infant fussing and minor accidents, indicating this occurs "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about infant safety occurring 'most days' with physical anxiety symptoms and compulsive checking, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic-like episodes (racing heart, breathlessness, impending doom) occurring spontaneously; fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent overwhelm, inability to manage daily tasks, and emotional exhaustion consistent with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to racing anxious thoughts and tearfulness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness with persistent low mood, tearfulness, and inability to sustain joy, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient reports multiple distress-related crying episodes triggered by everyday stressors, fitting "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple fleeting self-harm ideation episodes this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating high likelihood of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse core symptoms: depressed mood most of the time (<sym>gray cloud</sym>), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>no spark</sym>), fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt (<sym>it's my fault</sym>), sleep disruption, and recurrent thoughts of death. The prominence of <sym>anxiety</sym> and sudden <sym>panic symptoms</sym> also suggests comorbid perinatal <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or obstetrician for full evaluation
2. Ask about same-day referral to a perinatal mental health specialist or psychiatrist
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you develop a plan
4. Enlist a trusted adult to stay with you and help with baby care until professional safety plan is in place
5. Begin basic self-care: eat small regular snacks, sip water, rest when baby rests, accept household help without guilt
6. Consider evidence-based treatments your doctor may offer: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med>/<med>paroxetine</med> (compatible with breastfeeding)
7. Schedule follow-up within one week to monitor mood, anxiety, and safety plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 4–6 wk post-delivery; presents for routine mood screening.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, loss of enjoyment (Q1, Q2, Q8)  
- Daily tearfulness, crying spells (Q9)  
- Marked guilt / self-blame over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Intrusive, looping worries; panic symptoms without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Sleep initiation difficulty linked to ruminative thoughts (Q7)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning” in daily tasks (Q6)  
- Fleeting passive suicidal ideation (“what if I just weren’t here”) without plan or intent (Q10)

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety; functional impact evident (sleep, self-care, infant-care confidence).

Safety  
Passive SI present → safety risk flagged; immediate safety plan reviewed and referral to emergency services discussed if thoughts intensify or acquire intent/plan.

Screening impression  
High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; needs urgent psychiatric evaluation and coordinated care (OB, PCP, behavioral health).
